2.text: but a couple of men, and are used for short trips within the village range;

3.text: for instance, to catch dead seals floating on the surface or sunk to the bottom,

4.text: to go shooting water-fowl along the shore, to inspect the fish and seal nets, etc.

5.text: The frame of the large boat resembles that described by Nelson,¹ except

6.text: that the ribs and the cross-pieces of the bottom are set much closer together

7.text: (Fig. 44). The dimensions of the boat secured for our collection are, length,

8.text: 35 feet; breadth in the middle, between the gunwales, 4½ feet; breadth of

9.text: bottom in the middle, 2½ feet; height, 2 feet 8 inches. It has 21 cross-pieces,

10.text: and as many ribs on each side; 4 thwarts; 5 large oars and as many paddles.

11.text: It requires a crew of from six to eight men, and can carry freight up to two

12.text: tons. The central timber, strips and gunwales, according to the man who

13.text: sold me the boat, were brought from America in a rude state. The frame

14.text: was constructed on East Cape, and taken thence to Mečiˊwmɪn, and afterwards
14.note: it's the same name as in the lexicon

15.text: to Indian Point. At the last-named place it was covered with skin and used

16.text: for several years; so that, from the very circumstances regarding its construction,

17.text: it must be called typical for the Asiatic coast (Plate XI, Fig. 4). The home-

18.text: made boats of the Pacific villages between Indian Point and Anadyr, however,

19.text: are clumsier, and their sea qualities poorer.

20.text: The skin cover is unfastened for the winter and safely hidden from the

21.text: dogs. Late in the spring it is taken out and soaked for several days in

22.text: some pond or in the sea, though in the latter case the owner is obliged to

23.text: keep a sharp lookout for drifting ice and for the force of the current, which

24.text: may break the thongs by which it is secured and carry away the skin. The

25.text: work of covering is done by several persons; the boat’s crew, in order to

26.text: hasten matters, calling on their acquaintances and relatives to aid them. The

27.text: wet cover is pulled around the frame as tightly as possible, and its edge is

28.text: bent over the gunwale and laced to the middle strip with stout leather thongs.

29.text: After a while, when the lacings have dried a little, they are tightened by

30.text: means of walrus-tusks, which serve as marline-spike and hand-lever. Every

31.text: little hole in the skin is carefully patched and the boat turned bottom-side

32.text: up and allowed to dry for twenty-four hours. During this time it receives

33.text: two or three coatings of oil, and the patches are smeared around with thick oil-

34.text: drippings, at present more frequently with oil paints bought from whalers.

35.text: In former times boats were propelled by paddles (Fig. 45, a), and a large

36.text: broad-bladed paddle was used for steering (Fig. 45, b). At present, along

37.text: with the paddles, long narrow oars are used (Plate XI, Fig. 1). These are

38.text: imitations of the American whale-boat oars, and are often simply bought from

39.text: the whalers. Rowlocks, also copied from civilized designs, are fastened to the

40.text: skin covering. Each thwart has, for the most part, only one man, who rows in

41.text: civilized fashion. A rude helm (Fig. 45, c) has gradually replaced the steering-

42.text: paddle. It is curious that the oars of the Koryak boats, rest in loops instead
